title: Shipping
summary: Weeks 7–8. Make your AI apps production-ready and public: config and secrets, Docker, deploying to Railway or Render, CI with test and eval gates, logging and LLM tracing with cost tracking, auth, rate limits, caching and prompt caching. Project: ship all three earlier projects.

practice.question: You pushed a commit containing your `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` to a public GitHub repo, noticed, and pushed a commit deleting it five minutes later. What should you do first?
options: Nothing: the key is no longer in the latest commit
Rewrite the git history with `git filter-repo` so the key disappears
Revoke the key in the Claude Console, then create a new one and redeploy with it
Make the repository private
practice.explanation: The key is in the history, and bots scan public pushes within minutes, so assume it's been copied. Revoking it is the only step that stops it working. Then put a new key everywhere it's needed and redeploy. Cleaning history is optional once the key is dead.

practice.question: Why should the liveness check (`/health`) avoid querying the database or calling Claude?
options: Health checks must respond in under 1 ms
If a dependency has a brief problem, the platform would mark healthy app instances as dead and restart them, and calling Claude on every poll costs money
FastAPI doesn't allow database access in GET routes
Platforms send health checks without network access
practice.explanation: Liveness answers "is this process alive?". Tying it to the database or Claude turns a dependency blip into restarts of perfectly good instances, and a paid API call on every poll. Check dependencies in a separate readiness route (`/ready`) that returns 503.

practice.question: Your container logs `Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000`. You started it with `-p 8000:8000`, but `curl localhost:8000` on your Mac is refused. Why?
options: Port 8000 is reserved on macOS
Inside the container, 127.0.0.1 is the container's own loopback, so uvicorn only accepts connections from inside it; it must listen on 0.0.0.0
`-p` should be written `-p 127.0.0.1:8000`
The image needs `EXPOSE 8000` for `-p` to work
practice.explanation: Each container has its own network namespace. `127.0.0.1` there means the container itself, and forwarded traffic arrives on another interface. `--host 0.0.0.0` listens on all interfaces. `EXPOSE` is documentation only.

practice.question: Why does the Dockerfile copy `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` and run `uv sync` *before* `COPY . .`?
options: uv can't read files copied with `COPY . .`
So the slow dependency-install layer stays cached when only your code changes, and rebuilds take seconds
It makes the final image smaller
Docker requires dependency files to be copied first
practice.explanation: Docker reuses a cached layer only if that instruction and everything before it are unchanged. Your code changes on every build; dependencies rarely do. Installing them before copying the code keeps that layer cached.

practice.title: Guards for a public API: CORS and a body size limit

practice.question: Your API works perfectly from `curl`, but the React app on `https://myapp.com` gets a CORS error calling it. What's the fix?
options: Add `mode: "no-cors"` to the browser's fetch call
Add `https://myapp.com` to `allow_origins` in the API's `CORSMiddleware`
Switch the API from HTTPS to HTTP
Set `allow_origins=["*"]` so every site can call it
practice.explanation: CORS is enforced by browsers using headers your **server** sends. `curl` ignores CORS, which is why it worked. Allow the exact origin. `"*"` would let any website spend your money through its visitors' browsers, and `no-cors` just makes the response unreadable.

practice.question: You set Railway's healthcheck path to `/ready`. When does Railway call it?
options: Every 30 seconds for as long as the service runs
When a new deployment starts, before switching traffic to it; not after the deploy is live
Only when you click a button in the dashboard
On every incoming user request
practice.explanation: Railway uses the health check to decide when a new deployment can take traffic, and doesn't monitor it afterwards. For ongoing checks, use an external uptime monitor. (Render, by contrast, keeps checking and restarts unhealthy instances.)

practice.question: Your eval step prints `pass rate 62% (threshold 90%)`, yet the CI run is green. What's the most likely cause?
options: GitHub Actions ignores Python output
The eval script exits with code 0 whatever the score; CI only looks at exit codes
The threshold must be set in the YAML file
Pass rates under 70% are rounded up
practice.explanation: A step fails only when its command exits nonzero. The gate must turn "below threshold" into `sys.exit(1)`.

practice.question: Why does the main CI workflow (on every push and pull request) run tests with fakes instead of your real `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`?
options: GitHub forbids API keys in Actions
Real calls cost money on every push, are slow and flaky, and secrets aren't given to pull requests from forks, so those runs would fail
The Anthropic SDK doesn't work on Linux runners
Fakes are more accurate than the real model
practice.explanation: Tests should be free, fast and deterministic, and they must run on fork PRs, which don't receive secrets. Live evals against the real model go in a separate, manual or scheduled workflow with a CI-only key.

practice.question: Over an hour, 95 requests took 1 s and 5 took 30 s. Which number best describes what your slowest users experience?
options: The mean, 2.45 s
The p50 (median), 1 s
The p95, close to 30 s
The minimum, 1 s
practice.explanation: The mean describes nobody, and the median hides the slow tail. The p95 shows the experience of the slowest 5%, which is where complaints come from. Dashboard p50 and p95.

practice.question: In Langfuse's data model, what's the difference between a *span* and a *generation*?
options: A generation is a whole request; a span is one line of logs
Both are timed steps inside a trace, but a generation is an LLM call and carries model, token usage and cost
Spans are only for errors
Generations are scores given by users
practice.explanation: A trace is one request made of nested observations. A span is any timed unit of work (retrieval, a tool call); a generation is a span for a model call, with the extra fields Langfuse uses for cost and token dashboards. Scores are attached separately.

practice.title: Issue and verify hashed API keys

practice.question: Your system prompt starts with `Current time: {now}`, followed by a 10,000-token product manual with `cache_control` at its end. `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` is always 0. Why?
options: The manual is below the minimum cacheable length
The timestamp changes on every request, so the prefix before the breakpoint never matches exactly
Prompt caching only works on the `messages`, not the system prompt
You need to call a separate endpoint to read from the cache
practice.explanation: The cache is keyed on the exact prefix up to the breakpoint. Anything that varies must come **after** it: move the time into the user message (or drop it), and the manual becomes a stable, cacheable prefix.

practice.question: Why is a fast hash like SHA-256 acceptable for storing API keys you generated, but not for users' passwords?
options: SHA-256 is too slow for passwords
Generated keys are long and random, so there's nothing to guess; human passwords are short and guessable, so they need a deliberately slow hash like bcrypt or argon2
API keys don't need protecting
Passwords can't be hashed
practice.explanation: An attacker with the hashes can try billions of guesses per second against a fast hash. That finds human passwords quickly, but 256 random bits can't be guessed at any speed.

project.title: Ship it: production-ready and public
checklist: Each project reads config from environment variables through a validated `Settings` model and refuses to start when a variable is missing; `.env` is git-ignored and `.env.example` committed
`/health` (liveness) and `/ready` (503 when the database is down) on every service, open without a key
A `Dockerfile` (uv, slim base, dependencies before code, non-root user, `0.0.0.0:${PORT:-8000}`) and `.dockerignore` per project; `docker compose up --build` runs the app with pgvector
All three deployed on Railway or Render with public HTTPS URLs, health check paths set, secrets in platform variables, and a spend limit on the production key
GitHub Actions runs `pytest`, offline evals with a pass-rate gate, and a Docker build on every push and PR; these checks are required on `main`
JSON logs with request ids, and every LLM call traced (model, tokens, cost, latency, errors) in Langfuse or similar, plus an uptime monitor on `/health`
Per-client API keys stored as SHA-256 hashes, a token-bucket rate limit returning 429 with `Retry-After`, exact-origin CORS, body size limits and timeouts
Prompt caching confirmed with `cache_read_input_tokens`, a response cache for exact repeats, and a measured cost per request in each README
Each README has the live URL, a working `curl` example, a demo GIF, an architecture diagram, eval results and a CI badge
